hints: Focus on what actually breaks when a liquid boils, the forces between molecules, not the strong covalent bond inside each molecule.
Check the size similarity first. Count the total electrons in $\text{ICl}$ ($53+17$) and in $\text{Br}_2$ ($35+35$), and compare their $M_r$ values.
Now compare their polarity. One molecule is polar with an extra type of intermolecular force, and that explains the higher boiling point.
walkthrough:
**Remember what boiling point measures**

Boiling separates molecules from each other. It overcomes intermolecular forces between molecules.

It does NOT break the strong covalent bond within the molecule, so $\text{I-Cl}$ and $\text{Br-Br}$ bond energies are not relevant here.

**Compare size and electrons**

Both molecules are almost identical in size, so London dispersion forces will be very similar.

Total electrons: $\text{ICl} = 53 + 17 = 70$, $\text{Br}_2 = 35 + 35 = 70$
$$M_r(\text{ICl}) \approx 127 + 35.5 = 162.5$$
$$M_r(\text{Br}_2) \approx 80 + 80 = 159.8$$

**Compare polarity**

$\text{Br}_2$ is non-polar because both atoms are identical, so it has only instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (London) forces.

$\text{ICl}$ is polar because Cl is more electronegative than I, so it has $\text{I}^{\delta+}\text{-Cl}^{\delta-}$ and has permanent dipole-dipole forces in addition to London forces.

**Link to boiling point**

Stronger overall intermolecular forces need more energy to overcome, so give a higher boiling point.

$\text{ICl}$ has the extra permanent dipole-dipole attraction, so it boils higher than $\text{Br}_2$ despite similar mass and electron number.

options.A: Incorrect. Covalent bond energy is the strength of the intramolecular bond within the molecule. Boiling only breaks intermolecular forces between molecules, the covalent bonds stay intact, so this cannot explain the boiling point difference.
options.B: Correct. ICl is polar ($\text{I}^{\delta+}\text{-Cl}^{\delta-}$) and has permanent dipole-dipole forces plus London forces, while $\text{Br}_2$ is non-polar and has only London forces. The extra attraction in ICl requires more energy to separate, giving the higher boiling point.
options.C: Incorrect. This is a clever trap. Both species have exactly 70 electrons ($53+17$ for ICl and $35+35$ for Br2), so London forces due to electron number would be almost identical and cannot explain the difference.
options.D: Incorrect. The $M_r$ values are almost the same, about 162.5 for ICl and 159.8 for Br2. Such a tiny difference cannot account for the significantly higher boiling point of ICl.
